title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Reference, Packaging, Day-2 Ops, and Upgrade/Rollback Library
author: Elena Martinez
content:
Summary

This document is the canonical library for Redwood Inference private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It consolidates: reference architectures, packaging and distribution guidance, customer requirements checklists, day-2 operational procedures, and explicit upgrade and rollback playbooks. Use this page during presales, engagement planning, deployment execution, and oncall runbooks.

Scope and audience

- Audience: Solutions Engineers, Infra Engineers, Customer Engineering, SRE, and Sales Engineers.
- Scope: Supported VPC and on-prem patterns for Redwood Private (control plane + data plane), packaging formats, day-2 operational runbooks, upgrade/rollback procedures, and the customer requirements library used to validate readiness and acceptance.

Document structure

1) Reference architectures (diagram + patterns)
2) Packaging and distribution (artifacts, signing, versions)
3) Customer requirements and preflight checklist
4) Day-2 ops: monitoring, backups, scaling, and routine maintenance
5) Upgrade and rollback procedures (canary, in-place, blue/green)
6) Ownership, SLAs and escalation
7) Appendix: example configs, Terraform/Helm snippets, and troubleshooting tips

1) Reference architectures

Overview

Redwood Private supports two primary deployment tiers: VPC deployment (customer AWS/Azure/GCP environment, Redwood control plane integrated or customer-managed) and fully on-prem (air-gapped or customer datacenter). The following reference architectures are recommended starting points; adapt to customer constraints and security posture.

A. VPC deployment (recommended for most enterprise customers)

- Components: customer VPC (subnets: public/private), Bastion/Jumphost, Kubernetes cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS or self-managed), Redwood data plane (inference pods, autoscaler, KV cache), optional GPU node pools, Managed DB (Postgres) or customer-managed, object storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) for model artifacts, customer KMS for key management.
- Network flow: customer application -> internal API gateway -> Redwood inference service -> model cache -> GPU workers -> response. Control traffic to Redwood control plane over TLS and mTLS when required.
- Security: RBAC, network policies, NSGs/firewall rules; private endpoints (no public ingress to inference pods).

B. On-prem deployment (air-gapped or regulated environment)

- Components: Customer datacenter with Kubernetes (preferred), VLAN segmented network, local object storage (minio or vendor equivalent), HSM/KMS integration (optional), local registry for container images, offline model artifact distribution, NTP/CA/CRL distribution, and monitoring stack (Prometheus + Grafana).
- Packaging: deploy via signed Helm charts and offline tarballs. Provide an air-gap deployment package with checksums and GPG signatures.

C. Hybrid (control plane SaaS + local data plane)

- Use when customer requires local inference but allows Redwood control plane connectivity for orchestration and billing. Provide explicit egress rules and allowlist IP ranges.

Reference architecture table (summary)

| Pattern | Control plane | Data plane | Key constraints | Typical customer |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| VPC-managed | Redwood-hosted | Customer VPC | VPC peering, private endpoints, KMS | Enterprise SaaS |
| On-prem air-gapped | Customer-hosted | Customer datacenter | Offline packaging, HSM, no egress | Regulated / Gov |
| Hybrid | Redwood-hosted (or optional private control plane) | Customer edge | Strict egress allowlist, telemetry proxy | Low-latency inference + security |

2) Packaging and distribution

Artifacts produced by Redwood for private deployments:

- Helm charts (chart versioning semantic: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, e.g., 2.4.1)
- OCI/tarball container images with signed digests (sha256).
- Model bundles: sharded model artifact (.tar.gz) with manifest.json and checksums.
- Air-gap bundles: .tar.gz including Helm charts, images as tarballs, manifests, and install scripts.
- Release notes document and migration notes per version.

Signing and verification

- All artifacts are GPG signed (key id: 0xRDFW2028) and accompanied by SHA256 checksums. Customers must verify signature and checksum before installation. Provide example verification commands.

Example verification

1. Verify checksum: shasum -a 256 redwood-private-2.4.1.tar.gz
2. Verify signature: gpg --verify redwood-private-2.4.1.tar.gz.asc redwood-private-2.4.1.tar.gz

Version compatibility and matrix

- We maintain a compatibility matrix per release that maps control plane versions, data plane images, Helm chart versions, and supported Kubernetes minor versions (e.g., Kubernetes 1.25+ supported for data plane v2.x). See release compatibility table in the appendix.

3) Customer requirements and preflight checklist

Pre-install checklist (must be completed before deployment)

- Network
  - VPC/subnets provisioned (private subnets for inference), route tables, NAT Gateway as required.
  - Egress rules and allowlist for Redwood control plane IPs (if hybrid).
  - DNS entries and internal certificates (wildcard or per-service).
- Identity & secrets
  - KMS access configured (ARN for AWS KMS or equivalent).
  - Kubernetes service account permissions and admin user for initial install.
- Storage
  - Object store bucket created and lifecycle rules documented.
  - DB (Postgres) with backup snapshot schedule.
- Compute
  - GPU node pools sized to expected concurrency and model types.
  - Node taints/tolerations and resource classes defined.
- Security and compliance
  - SOC2/PXI review signoff if required for customer.
  - HSM integration plan for customers requiring FIPS-level key storage.
- Operational readiness
  - Monitoring endpoints and metrics collection (Prometheus scrape targets)
  - SRE oncall rotation and escalation contact list

Preflight validation checklist (commands and tests)

1) Verify cluster connectivity: kubectl get nodes --context <ctx>
2) Verify storage access: aws s3 ls s3://<bucket>
3) Verify image pulls (for air-gap, load images locally and validate): docker load < image.tar.gz; docker inspect <image>
4) Run smoke test: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh --endpoint <internal-lb>

4) Day-2 operations

Monitoring and alerting (suggested SLI/SLOs)

- SLIs we collect: p95 tail latency (inference), request success rate (2xx), model load time, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate.
- Default SLOs for typical production app:
  - Availability: 99.9% (monthly) for dedicated clusters
  - p95 latency: <= 250ms for small models; <= 800ms for large models (subject to model profile)
  - Error budget policy: alert when error rate exceeds 0.1% over 15 minutes

Alert thresholds (example)

- GPU memory utilization > 90% for 5m -> paged to SRE
- KV cache miss rate > 30% for 10m -> investigate model sharding/config
- Pod restart rate > 5 restarts in 15m -> oncall page
- Control plane heartbeat missing > 2m for hybrid -> page escalation team

Routine maintenance tasks

- Weekly: rotate short-lived API keys, audit role bindings, verify backups completed.
- Monthly: reconcile model artifact storage, test disaster recovery snapshot restore in staging.
- Quarterly: exercise upgrade in staging per the upgrade playbook.

Backup and DR

- Postgres automated snapshots (daily), object store replication policy (recommended 30-day retention), model artifact retention policy per customer SLA.
- DR exercise procedure: restore Postgres from latest snapshot to staging, rehydrate object store, run smoke tests; target RTO in staging: 4 hours.

Capacity and autoscaling guidance

- Continuous batching and autoscaler parameters are configured in the Helm chart. Suggested starting values:
  - minReplicas: 3
  - maxReplicas: 20
  - targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60
  - custom metric: targetTokensPerSecond per GPU (varies by model)

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures

Overview

We support three upgrade strategies depending on customer risk tolerance and environment: in-place rolling upgrades (Kubernetes best effort), canary (traffic splitting), and blue/green (parallel data plane). For air-gap/on-prem customers, the same strategies apply but require additional artifact staging verification. Always perform an upgrade in non-production first.

Pre-upgrade prerequisites

- Current backup snapshot exists and verification that restore succeeds (test restore within the last 7 days).
- Release notes reviewed; breaking changes identified and mitigations planned.
- Compatibility matrix checked and validated.
- Oncall engineer and solutions engineer present or on slack for real-time escalation.

Canary upgrade procedure (recommended for low-risk changes)

1) Stage new Helm chart and images in a staging namespace and run integration smoke tests.
2) Deploy new version to a small subset of pods (create canary deployment label: redwood-inference=canary).
3) Configure traffic split at gateway (example: 5% canary / 95% production) and run load test for 30-60 minutes.
4) Monitor SLIs: error rate, latency, GPU OOMs, KV cache behavior.
5) If checks pass, increment traffic 25% every 15 minutes until 100%. If failures occur, follow rollback steps below.

Rolling in-place upgrade procedure

1) Set pod disruption budget to ensure capacity.
2) Perform a rolling upgrade via Helm: helm upgrade --install redwood-private ./chart --namespace redwood --set image.tag=2.5.0 --wait --timeout 15m
3) Watch pod readiness and rollout status: kubectl rollout status deployment/redwood-inference --namespace redwood
4) Validate with smoke tests after each deployment batch (recommended batch size: 10-20% of pods).

Blue/Green upgrade procedure (highest isolation)

1) Deploy new data plane into a parallel namespace (redwood-green).
2) Run full staging tests including long-running inference and model loading.
3) Switch network routing at the ingress/gateway level when green is verified.
4) Keep old (blue) environment available for immediate rollback; teardown after 48 hours once metrics are stable.

Rollback procedure (common for all upgrade types)

1) Trigger rollback in orchestration: kubectl rollout undo deployment/redwood-inference --namespace redwood --to-revision=<previous-revision> OR helm rollback redwood-private <revision>
2) If traffic split was used, instantly shift traffic back to previous replica set.
3) If stateful changes occurred (DB migrations), run migration rollback plan documented in the release note (some migrations are irreversible; in those cases restore DB from backup and rehydrate).
4) Post-mortem: capture timeline, metrics, and root cause; notify stakeholders.

Validation and smoke tests (post-upgrade)

- Run the full smoke test suite: ./tests/smoke/full-suite.sh --env=prod --parallel 10
- Verify KV cache hit rate within acceptable delta compared to baseline.
- Verify model predictions on a set of golden prompts to detect regressions.

6) Ownership, SLAs and escalation

Operational ownership

- Customer Engineering: coordinates deployment, network, and security tasks.
- Redwood SRE: owns monitoring, alerting, runbooks, and emergency rollback actions.
- Product Engineering: owns data plane images and change design; assists with complex rollbacks.

Escalation matrix (summary)

- P0 (system down) -> SRE primary (pager) -> SRE lead -> Engineering director -> Exec oncall within 60 minutes.
- P1 (severe degradation) -> SRE primary -> Customer Engineering -> Solutions Eng.

Communication templates

- Outage notification template (email/Slack): include impact, affected services, ETA, mitigation steps, and owner. Keep updates every 30 minutes for P0 until resolved.

7) Appendix: example configs, snippets and troubleshooting

Example Helm values excerpt (YAML)

# values.yaml excerpt
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: registry.redwood-inference/private-data-plane
  tag: 2.5.0
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "16Gi"
    cpu: "4000m"
  limits:
    memory: "32Gi"
    cpu: "8000m"

Example Terraform snippet (VPC peering, AWS)

resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "redwood_peering" {
  vpc_id        = var.customer_vpc_id
  peer_vpc_id   = var.redwood_vpc_id
  auto_accept   = true
  tags = {
    Name = "redwood-peer-${var.customer_name}"
  }
}

Troubleshooting checklist (common failures)

- Pod OOMs: check model size, GPU memory limits, and batch sizes. Consider model quantization profile.
- High latency: inspect GPU saturation, network bandwidth, and batch/queueing configuration.
- Control plane disconnects: verify allowlist, TLS certs, and control plane IPs.
